title: Write and present for a wide range of purposes, audiences and contexts

lessons.title: Planning and writing for purpose and audience
lessons.html:
Start with purpose and audience

Every piece of writing has a purpose and an audience. Before you write, answer three questions:

  • Why am I writing? To inform, to instruct, to persuade, to request, to record or to report.
  • Who will read it? An overseas buyer, a PPECB inspector, packhouse staff, a bank manager or the board of a growers' company.
  • What do they need to do with it? Make a decision, follow a procedure, approve a budget or simply be informed.

A quality report for an importer must be factual and precise; a notice for packhouse workers must be short, simple and possibly in more than one language; a proposal for a new cold store must persuade with evidence.

Common workplace documents

DocumentKey features
EmailClear subject line, one main topic, short paragraphs, action required stated
ReportTitle, summary, introduction, findings, conclusions, recommendations, appendices
Procedure or work instructionNumbered steps, one action per step, warnings before the step they apply to
ProposalProblem, proposed solution, costs and benefits, risks, request
MinutesDate, attendees, decisions, actions with owners and dates
Claim responseFacts, evidence such as temperature records, position, proposed resolution

The writing process

  1. Gather facts and evidence.
  2. Plan the structure with headings.
  3. Draft without worrying about perfection.
  4. Revise for clarity, logic and tone: remove unnecessary words, check that each paragraph has one main idea.
  5. Edit and proofread for spelling, grammar, figures, names and dates.

Style

Use plain language, active voice and specific words. Write the cold room reached 4 degrees at 14:00, not temperature issues were experienced. Keep a professional, courteous tone, even in a complaint. Be careful with abbreviations: an overseas reader may not know what PUC or PHC means. Check facts and figures twice: a wrong pallet number or temperature in a report can cost money and credibility.

lessons.title: Presenting information effectively
lessons.html:
Preparing a presentation

Managers present often: a season review to growers, a quality briefing to packhouse supervisors, a proposal to the board, or a market report to visiting buyers. Preparation follows the same logic as writing.

  1. Define the purpose: what should the audience know, feel or do at the end?
  2. Analyse the audience: their knowledge, language, interests and concerns. Growers want to know about returns; supervisors want practical changes; a bank wants risk and repayment.
  3. Structure the content: an opening that states the purpose, three to five main points supported by evidence, and a conclusion that summarises and states the action required.
  4. Choose visual aids: simple slides, charts, samples of fruit or packaging, or handouts.
  5. Rehearse aloud and time yourself.

Using visual aids well

  • One idea per slide, with few words and large text.
  • Use charts to show trends, such as packout percentages per week, rather than tables of numbers.
  • Label axes and units clearly.
  • Real examples, such as a carton with a marking error or a photograph of a defect, are powerful.
  • Have a back-up plan if the projector or power fails.

Delivery

  • Speak clearly and at a steady pace; pause after important points.
  • Make eye contact and face the audience, not the screen.
  • Use examples and stories from the farm or packhouse.
  • Adapt your language to the audience; explain technical terms.
  • Be aware of different cultures and languages in the room, and check understanding.

Handling questions

Listen to the whole question, repeat it if the room is large, and answer briefly. If you do not know the answer, say so and promise to follow up, then do it. Stay calm with challenging questions; acknowledge concerns and refer to evidence.

Evaluating your communication

Afterwards, ask for feedback and check whether the purpose was achieved: did the board approve the proposal, did supervisors apply the new procedure? Use what you learn to improve next time.

Key points

  • Define purpose and audience before writing or presenting.
  • Choose the right document format and structure.
  • Draft, revise, edit and proofread, checking facts and figures.
  • Keep slides simple and use real examples and clear charts.
  • Rehearse, adapt to the audience and handle questions honestly.
